svg.text: Primary and its HA replicas — one database name, one SLO
the only node that writes log
Named replicas — up to 30, each a database of its own
Named replica 1 — with HA replicas of its own
these HA replicas follow the named replica,
one log stream · no replica is in the commit path
— one copy of the data, shared by every replica above
log for redo — one stream to all
· The hottest pages across the compute
replicas are tracked, and that list is used
to fill each HA replica's buffer pool and
· So a secondary is already warm when it
becomes the failover or the read target.
· It works both ways: the primary caches
what is hot on the secondaries too.
· One copy of the data. Every box above reads the
same page servers — there is no second copy.
· Adding one copies nothing. It is compute attached
· Compute-only billing — storage costs do not apply
· None is in the commit path, so commit latency does
not grow as you add replicas.
Where the two kinds part company — and how reads reach them
· Same server, same database name, always its parent's SLO. The failover target.
· Reached only by ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly on that same connection string;
it gets no endpoint of its own. With several, a read-only connection lands on
an arbitrary one — the service does no intelligent load balancing.
· Continuous priming keeps its buffer pool and RBPEX hot (provisioned tier).
· Its own name, endpoint, SLO and logins; always read-only, so no ApplicationIntent.
· Nothing spreads reads across them for you — the app picks which one to call.
· The green stack inside the purple frame is the
point: a named replica is itself a parent. Its HA
replicas inherit from it, not from the primary.
· A named replica starts with none, like the second.
· Azure Storage is absent on purpose. No compute
node in this figure ever reaches it.
· Only the primary has an arrow pointing down into
the log service. Everyone else only receives.
Continuous priming (two-way, parent to its own HA replicas)
